rationale: B wins because it understands the ugly part of the story, not just the launch wrapper. Its angle, "Substack's video feed raises a question for writers who never wanted to be on camera," gives a reporter tension, a protagonist, and a hard company question. A has useful bones, but "Substack completes its swap from email newsletter to all-in-video media app" overstates the facts so hard it starts pitching the movie trailer, not the story.
gaps_in_A: "Substack completes its swap from email newsletter to all-in-video media app" is overcooked. The update supports native video and a media-app strategy, not a completed swap or an all-in-video company.
"short-form, algorithmic-style feed" adds mechanics not supplied. The fact block says TikTok-style feed; algorithmic ranking is exactly the thing A should ask about, not assert.

"The numbers behind Substack's 'struggling platform' reputation don't add up" is too declarative for the evidence. The $400M creator aggregate and 4M paid subscriptions do not by themselves disprove funding problems.
The funding and contrarian angles share the same spine: funding struggles plus disclosed scale. They are separable, but A has to work too hard to keep them apart.
gaps_in_B: "Substack is done being a newsletter company" still overstates the pivot. Better than A's "all-in-video," but it needs to stay framed as a question, not a verdict.
"One writer's case for moving video and podcasts onto Substack under a 10% cut" is conditional on a named creator. B admits that in proof, but without that person this angle does not exist.
"The feature is live today" is a reasonable inference from the supplied current-time launch context, but it should be treated as launch-day wording, not a sourced fact if the pitch goes out later.
"Next step: meanest-editor" is the wrong operational handoff for an angle set. The sharper next move is to pick the angle, secure proof, then build a fit-checked journalist list.
